content: 1. Healthy eating patterns during childhood and adolescence are essential for promoting optimal health, growth, and intellectual development. They help prevent immediate health issues such as iron deficiency anemia, obesity, eating disorders, and dental caries, and may also reduce the risk of long-term health problems like coronary heart disease, cancer, and stroke. 2. School health programs can support children and adolescents in achieving their full educational potential and maintaining good health by equipping them with the skills, social support, and environmental reinforcement necessary to adopt long-term healthy eating behaviors. 3. This report outlines strategies that are most effective in promoting healthy eating among school-aged youth and provides nutrition education guidelines for a comprehensive school health program. 4. These guidelines are based on a thorough review of research, theoretical frameworks, and current practices. They were developed by the CDC in collaboration with experts from universities, national organizations, federal agencies, and voluntary groups. 5. The guidelines include recommendations on seven key aspects of school-based programs to promote healthy eating: school nutrition policies, a sequential and coordinated curriculum, appropriate student instruction, integration of school food services with nutrition education, staff training, family and community involvement, and program evaluation. 6. School-based programs play a critical role in fostering lifelong healthy eating habits. 7. Dietary factors significantly contribute to the burden of preventable illnesses and premature deaths in the United States. National health promotion and disease prevention objectives encourage schools to provide nutrition education from preschool through 12th grade. 8. The USDA's Nutrition Education and Training (NET) Program emphasizes that nutrition education should be a major component of all child nutrition programs and should be offered in all schools, childcare facilities, and summer sites. 9. Since diet influences both learning potential and health, the first national education goal includes ensuring that children receive the nutrition and healthcare needed to arrive at school with healthy minds and bodies. 10. The recommendations in this report aim to assist school personnel and policymakers at various levels in meeting national health objectives and education goals by implementing school-based nutrition education policies and programs. 11. This report may also serve as a resource for students, parents, and professionals in local and state health departments, community-based health and nutrition programs, pediatric clinics, and training institutions for teachers and public health professionals. 12. These recommendations complement CDC guidelines for school health programs aimed at preventing the spread of AIDS, reducing tobacco use and addiction, and promoting physical activity. 13. In this report, nutrition education encompasses a wide range of activities designed to encourage healthy eating behaviors. 14. The nutrition education guidelines primarily focus on classroom instruction but are relevant to all components of a comprehensive school health program, including health education, a healthy environment, health services, counseling, integrated school-community efforts, physical education, nutrition services, and school-based health promotion for staff. 15. While school food service programs play a vital role in school health programs, this report does not provide specific recommendations on food purchasing and preparation for school meals. Detailed information on this topic is available in other publications. 16. These guidelines do not address the specific nutrition education and counseling needs of pregnant adolescents or young individuals with special needs. 17. The guidelines are based on a synthesis of research, theory, and current practices and align with the principles of national health education standards, opportunity-to-learn standards for health education, and recommendations from leading child nutrition organizations. 18. To develop these guidelines, the CDC convened meetings with nutrition education experts, reviewed published research, considered national policy recommendations, and consulted with experts from various organizations. 19. School-based nutrition education can improve dietary practices that influence the health, growth, and intellectual development of young individuals. 20. Immediate effects of unhealthy eating patterns include undernutrition, iron deficiency anemia, and overweight and obesity. 21. Even moderate undernutrition can have lasting effects on children's cognitive development and school performance. 22. Chronically undernourished children tend to score lower on standardized achievement tests, particularly in language ability. 23. Hunger and undernutrition make children more susceptible to infections, leading to increased school absences and academic setbacks. They also cause irritability, difficulty concentrating, and low energy levels, which can hinder learning and physical activity. 24. 25. Skipping breakfast negatively impacts children's performance in problem-solving tasks. 26. Participation in the School Breakfast Program has been associated with improved standardized test scores and reduced rates of absenteeism and tardiness among low-income elementary school students. 27. National surveys indicate that a significant proportion of students skip breakfast, with many eating breakfast on two or fewer days per week. 28. Strategies to promote adequate nutrition among young individuals include encouraging participation in USDA food assistance programs, advising parents about community-based food supplementation programs, and educating students and families about the importance of eating breakfast. 29. Iron deficiency anemia is the most common cause of anemia in the United States and impairs the body's ability to produce hemoglobin, which is essential for oxygen transport in the blood. 30. Iron deficiency can lead to fatigue, reduced attention span, decreased work capacity, lower resistance to infection, and impaired intellectual performance. 31. Female adolescents are at the highest risk for iron deficiency, with 2%-4% of girls aged 12-19 years showing evidence of iron deficiency anemia. 32. To prevent iron deficiency, children and adolescents should consume adequate amounts of iron-rich foods and vitamin C, which enhances iron absorption. 33. Overweight and obesity are increasing among children and adolescents in the United States, with the prevalence of overweight more than doubling in the past 30 years. 34. 35. Being overweight during childhood and adolescence is linked to increased adult mortality and psychological stress due to social exclusion and discrimination. 36. Increased physical activity and appropriate caloric intake are recommended for preventing and reducing obesity. 37. Many young individuals in the United States engage in unsafe weight-loss methods, such as meal skipping, fasting, and using diet pills or laxatives. 38. Unsafe weight-loss practices can lead to poor growth, delayed sexual development, and other health risks. 39. Adolescents involved in competitive sports and dancing are particularly at risk for unsafe weight control practices. 40. Children and adolescents should be educated about the dangers of unsafe weight-loss methods and the importance of maintaining a healthy body image. 41. Eating disorders, such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, are severe psychological conditions characterized by disturbances in eating behavior. 42. Eating disorders often begin during adolescence and predominantly affect females, with up to 3% of adolescent and young adult females affected. 43. Eating disorders are associated with low self-esteem, negative body image, and severe complications, including high mortality rates. 44. Immediate medical and psychological treatment is essential for individuals with eating disorders. 45. Dental caries is one of the most prevalent diseases, affecting a significant proportion of children and adolescents. 46. Untreated dental caries can lead to acute infections, pain, costly treatments, and tooth loss. 47. To prevent dental caries, children and adolescents should drink fluoridated water, use fluoridated toothpaste, brush and floss regularly, and consume sugars in moderation. 48. Nutrition education should focus on preventing chronic diseases in adulthood, as many diet-related risk factors begin in childhood. 49. Early indicators of atherosclerosis, a major cause of coronary heart disease, are related to blood cholesterol levels in young individuals. 50. Poor diet and inadequate physical activity contribute to at least 300,000 deaths annually in the United States and are second only to tobacco use as a preventable cause of premature death. 51. Interventions promoting healthy eating and physical activity during childhood and adolescence can prevent leading causes of illness and death, reduce healthcare costs, and improve quality of life. 52. Diet is a known risk factor for coronary heart disease, cancer, and stroke, the nation's three leading causes of death. 53. 54. 55. Cancer accounts for one in five deaths in the United States, with dietary factors linked to several types of cancer, including colon, breast, and prostate cancer. 56. 57. Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States and is often associated with obesity. 58. 59. Osteoporosis, characterized by severe bone loss, increases the risk of fractures, particularly in older adults. 60. Regular weight-bearing exercises and adequate calcium intake during childhood and adolescence are crucial for preventing osteoporosis later in life.
